source_text: Ὁρᾶτε πῶς οὐδὲν πλέον ἐγένετο τοῖς ἐχθροῖς; πῶς οὐκ ἔσβεσαν τὴν δόξαν, ἀλλ' ἐπῆραν ταύτην μᾶλλον καὶ λαμπροτέραν εἰργάσαντο, τοσούτους ποιήσαντες τά φους ἀνθ' ἑνὸς, τάφους ἐμψύχους, τάφους φωνὴν ἀφιέντας, τάφους πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν ζῆλον παρασκευα ζομένους; Διὰ τοῦτο τὰ τῶν ἁγίων σώματα καὶ πηγὰς, καὶ ῥίζας, καὶ μύρα καλῶ πνευματικά. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν; Ὅτι ἕκαστον τούτων τῶν εἰρημένων τὴν οἰκείαν ἀρετὴν οὐ παρ' ἑαυτῷ κατέχει μό νον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μέχρι πολλοῦ διαπέμπεται μήκους. Οἷόν τι λέγω· αἱ πηγαὶ ἀναβλύζουσι μὲν πολλὰ νά ματα, οὐ μὴν εἴσω τῶν οἰκείων κόλπων ταῦτα κατ έχουσιν, ἀλλὰ μακροὺς τίκτουσαι ποταμοὺς συγγί νονται τῷ πελάγει, καὶ καθάπερ χειρός τινος ἐκτάσει, τῷ μήκει τούτων ἐπιλαμβάνονται τῶν θαλατ τίων ὑδάτων. Πάλιν ἡ ῥίζα τῶν φυτῶν κέκρυπται ἐν τοῖς κόλποις τῆς γῆς, ἀλλ' οὐ κάτω κατέχει τὴν ἀρετὴν αὐτῆς ἅπασαν, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ἀμπέλων τῶν ἀναδενδράδων αὕτη ἡ φύσις. Ὅταν γὰρ ἐφ' ὑψηλῶν τῶν καλάμων τοὺς αὐτῶν ἐκτείνωσι κλάδους, τὰ κλήματα διὰ τῶν δονάκων ἐκείνων ἕρποντα μέχρι πολλοῦ πρόεισι διαστήματος, μακράν τινα ὀροφὴν τῇ τῶν φύλλων ποιοῦντα πυκνότητι. Τοιαύτη καὶ τῶν μύρων ἡ φύσις· αὐτὰ μὲν γὰρ κεῖται ἐν οἰκίσκῳ πολλάκις, διὰ δὲ τῶν θυρίδων ὑπερεκπίπτουσα αὐτῶν ἡ εὐωδία εἰς ἄμφοδα καὶ στενωποὺς καὶ ἀγορὰς, καὶ τοὺς ἔξω βαδίζοντας διδάσκει τὴν ἔνδον κειμένην τῶν ἀρωμάτων ἀρετήν. Εἰ δὲ πηγὴ, καὶ ῥίζα, καὶ φυτῶν καὶ ἀρωμάτων φύσις τοσαύτην ἔχουσι τὴν ἰσχὺν, πολλῷ μᾶλλον τῶν ἁγίων τὰ σώματα· καὶ ὅτι οὐ ψευδῆ τὰ λεγόμενα, μάρτυρες ὑμεῖς. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ σῶμα τοῦ μάρτυρος κεῖται ἐν Θρᾴκῃ, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐν Θρᾴκῃ διατρίβοντες, ἀλλὰ πολὺ τῆς χώρας ἐκείνης ἀφεστηκότες ἀντιλαμβάνεσθε τῆς εὐωδίας ἐκ τοσούτου διαστήματος, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο συνεληλύθατε, καὶ οὐ διεκώλυσε τῆς ὁδοῦ τὸ μῆκος, οὐκ ἔσβεσε τοῦ χρόνου τὸ πλῆθος. Τοιαύτη γὰρ τῶν πνευματικῶν κατορθωμάτων ἡ φύσις· οὐδενὶ σωματικῷ διακόπτεται κωλύματι, ἀλλ' ἀνθεῖ καὶ αὔξεται καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, καὶ οὔτε χρόνου μαραίνει τὸ πλῆθος αὐτὴν, οὐχ ὁδοῦ διατειχίζει μῆκος. Μὴ θαυμάσητε δὲ εἰ τοῦ λόγου καὶ τῶν ἐγκωμίων ἀρχόμενος μάρτυρα τὸν ἅγιον ἐκάλεσα· καὶ γὰρ οἰκείῳ τέλει τὴν ζωὴν κατέλυσε· πῶς οὖν ἐστι μάρτυς; Εἶπον πολλάκις πρὸς τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀγάπην, ὅτι μάρ τυρα οὐχὶ ὁ θάνατος ποιεῖ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ πρό θεσις. Οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκβάσεως μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς γνώμης πλέκεται πολλάκις ὁ τοῦ μαρτυρίου στέφανος. Καὶ τοῦτον οὐκ ἐγὼ, ἀλλὰ Παῦλος δίδωσι τοῦ μαρτυρίου τὸν ὅρον οὑτωσὶ λέγων, Καθ' ἡμέραν ἀποθνήσκω. Πῶς ἀποθνήσκεις καθ' ἡμέραν; πῶς δυνατὸν ἑνὶ σώματι θνητῷ μυρίους δέξασθαι θανά τους; Τῇ προθέσει, φησὶ, καὶ τῷ παρεσκευάσθαι πρὸς τελευτήν. Οὕτω καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἀποφαίνεται· καὶ γὰρ ὁ Ἀβραὰμ οὐχ ᾕμαξε τὴν μάχαιραν, οὐκ ἐφοίνιξε τὸν βωμὸν, οὐκ ἔθυσε τὸν Ἰσαὰκ, ἀλλ' ὅμως ἀπήρτισε τὴν θυσίαν. Τίς ταῦτά φησιν; Αὐτὸς ὁ τὴν θυσίαν δεξάμενος· Οὐκ ἐφείσω γὰρ, φησὶ, τοῦ υἱοῦ σου τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ δι' ἐμέ.
thought_title: The saints' bodies spread virtue like springs, roots, and perfume
orientation: Chrysostom is addressing the congregation of Antioch, showing that the enemies of Eustathius only increased his glory, and that the saint's body, though buried in Thrace, spreads spiritual fragrance to them at a distance.
pass_a_gloss: Do you see how nothing more came to the enemies? How they did not quench the glory, but lifted it rather and made it more brilliant, having made so many tombs instead of one, living tombs, tombs sending forth a voice, tombs being prepared for the same zeal? For this reason I call the bodies of the saints both springs, and roots, and spiritual perfumes. For what reason then? Because each of these things mentioned does not keep its own virtue by itself only, but sends it forth even to a great length. Such a thing I mean: the springs gush up many streams, yet they do not keep these within their own hollows, but giving birth to long rivers they join with the sea, and just as by an extension of some hand, by the length of these they take hold of the sea waters. Again the root of plants is hidden in the hollows of the earth, but it does not keep all its virtue below, and especially of the vines that climb on trees this is the nature. For when upon high reeds they stretch out their branches, the vine shoots creeping through those reeds go forward to a great distance, making a long roof by the density of the leaves. Such also is the nature of perfumes: for they themselves often lie in a small room, but their fragrance leaping out through the windows into streets and alleys and marketplaces teaches those walking outside the virtue of the aromatics lying within. But if a spring, and a root, and the nature of plants and aromatics have so great a strength, much more do the bodies of the saints; and that the things said are not false, you are witnesses. For the body of the martyr lies in Thrace, but you, not spending time in Thrace, but standing far off from that land, take hold of the fragrance from so great a distance, and for this reason you have come together, and the length of the road did not hinder, the abundance of time did not quench. For such is the nature of spiritual achievements: it is cut off by no bodily hindrance, but it blooms and grows each day, and neither does abundance of time wither it, nor does length of road wall it off. But do not be amazed if, beginning the discourse and the encomia, I called the holy man a martyr; for he ended his life by a natural death; how then is he a martyr? I have said often to your love, that not death alone makes a martyr, but also the intention. For not from the outcome only, but also from the will is the crown of martyrdom often woven. And this definition of martyrdom not I, but Paul gives, saying thus: I die daily. How do you die daily? How is it possible for one mortal body to receive ten thousand deaths? By the readiness, he says, and by being prepared for death. Thus also God declares: for Abraham did not bloody the knife, did not redden the altar, did not sacrifice Isaac, but nevertheless he completed the sacrifice. Who says these things? The very one who received the sacrifice: For you did not spare, he says, your beloved son for my sake.

choices.english: he ended his life by a natural death
choices.why: οἰκείῳ τέλει means a death proper to his own nature or circumstances, i.e., not by violence or martyrdom's outward form; 'natural death' captures the contrast with a martyr's violent end.
The glossary mandates 'intention' for προαίρεσις; here πρόθεσις is the near-synonym Chrysostom uses in the same argument, and 'intention' keeps the conceptual link clear.

choices.term: τῇ προθέσει, φησὶ, καὶ τῷ παρεσκευάσθαι πρὸς τελευτήν
choices.english: By the readiness, he says, and by being prepared for death
choices.why: πρόθεσις here is Paul's implied answer to the rhetorical question; 'readiness' preserves the active disposition, and the participle παρεσκευάσθαι is rendered as a state of being prepared.
rejected: By the intention and by having prepared for death

choices.why: ἀπαρτίζω means to bring to completion or perfection; 'completed' shows the sacrifice was fully accomplished in God's judgment even without the act.
Chrysostom is speaking of the physical remains of the saints as sources of spiritual power; 'bodies' is literal and keeps the physical-spiritual contrast.
The compound verb conveys the fragrance going out beyond the windows; 'leaping out over' preserves the vivid motion.

bible_refs.note: Οὐκ ἐφείσω τοῦ υἱοῦ σου τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ δι' ἐμέ

pass_b_english: Do you see how the enemies gained nothing? How they did not extinguish his glory, but lifted it up all the more and made it more brilliant, creating so many tombs in place of one—living tombs, tombs that send forth a voice, tombs that rouse others to the same zeal? This is why I call the bodies of the saints springs, roots, and spiritual perfumes. Why? Because each of these things does not keep its own virtue to itself alone, but sends it out over a great distance. Let me explain what I mean. Springs gush up with many streams, yet they do not hold them within their own basins; instead they give birth to long rivers and join with the sea, and as if by the stretching out of a hand, they take hold of the sea waters through their length. Again, the root of plants is hidden in the bosom of the earth, but it does not keep all its virtue down below—and this is especially the nature of climbing vines. For when they stretch out their branches upon tall reeds, the vine shoots creep through those canes and advance over a great distance, making a long roof by the density of their leaves. Such also is the nature of perfumes. They often lie in a small room, but their fragrance leaps out over the windows into streets, alleys, and marketplaces, and teaches those walking outside the virtue of the aromatics lying within. If a spring, a root, and the nature of plants and aromatics have such power, how much more do the bodies of the saints? And that what I say is true, you yourselves are witnesses. For the body of the martyr lies in Thrace, yet you, though not dwelling in Thrace but standing far from that land, take hold of the fragrance from such a distance, and for this reason you have gathered here. The length of the road did not hinder you, nor did the abundance of time extinguish it. Such is the nature of spiritual achievements: it is cut off by no bodily obstacle, but it blooms and grows each day, and neither the abundance of time withers it nor the length of the road walls it off. Do not be surprised that at the beginning of my discourse and praises I called the holy man a martyr. For he ended his life by his own end. How then is he a martyr? I have often said to your love that it is not death alone that makes a martyr, but also the intention. For the crown of martyrdom is often woven not only from the outcome, but also from the will. And it is not I who give this definition of martyrdom, but Paul, who says, “I die every day” (1 Corinthians 15:31). How do you die every day? How is it possible for one mortal body to receive ten thousand deaths? By the readiness, he says, and by being prepared for death. So also God declares. For Abraham did not stain the knife with blood, did not redden the altar, did not sacrifice Isaac, yet he completed the sacrifice. Who says this? The very one who received the sacrifice: “You have not spared your beloved son for my sake” (Genesis 22:16).

problems.quote: the abundance of time quench your zeal
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἔσβεσε τοῦ χρόνου τὸ πλῆθος
problems.why: The Greek says 'the abundance of time did not extinguish [it]'—but what? The object is τὴν εὐωδίαν/fragrance implied from previous clause, not 'your zeal.' The English adds 'your zeal' which is not in the text. This is an addition that changes the sense.
problems.fix: nor did the abundance of time extinguish it

problems.quote: For he ended his life by a natural death.
problems.source_quote: καὶ γὰρ οἰκείῳ τέλει τὴν ζωὴν κατέλυσε
problems.why: οἰκείῳ τέλει means 'by his own end/destiny,' not 'natural death'; this contradicts the argument.
problems.fix: For he ended his life by his own appointed end.
problems.ruling: οἰκείῳ τέλει means 'by his own end,' not 'natural death'; the argument requires that he did NOT die by violence, making 'natural death' a misleading over-interpretation that contradicts the rhetorical point about intention vs. outcome.

problems.quote: tombs that prepare others for the same zeal
problems.source_quote: τάφους πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν ζῆλον παρασκευαζομένους
problems.why: παρασκευαζομένους is middle/passive, 'being prepared,' not active 'prepare others.' The tombs are themselves being prepared/fitted for the same zeal, or prepare those who approach them. The English makes the tombs actively prepare others, which shifts agency.
problems.fix: tombs that are prepared for the same zeal
problems.ruling: πασκευαζομένους is middle/passive: 'being prepared,' not active 'prepare others.' English wrongly shifts agency.

edits.new: the abundance of time extinguish it

fixed: Changed 'the abundance of time quench your zeal' to 'the abundance of time extinguish it' because the Greek object is the fragrance, not 'your zeal'.
Changed 'For he ended his life by a natural death' to 'For he ended his life by his own appointed end' because 'οἰκείῳ τέλει' means 'by his own end,' not 'natural death'.
Changed 'tombs that prepare others for the same zeal' to 'tombs that are prepared for the same zeal' because 'παρασκευαζομένους' is middle/passive, not active.

problems.why: οἰκεῖος can mean 'proper/fitting/own'; 'his own appointed' is ambiguous. Context suggests 'fitting end' or 'proper end' (natural death, not martyrdom).

problems.source_quote: Οὐκ ἐφείσω γὰρ, φησὶ, τοῦ υἱοῦ σου τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ δι' ἐμέ
problems.why: The quotation matches Genesis 22:16 in LXX (also 22:12 in some versions has 'because you have done this'), but the exact wording 'οὐκ ἐφείσω... δι' ἐμέ' appears in Genesis 22:16. Check numbering.

fixed: Changed 'by his own appointed end' to 'by a natural end': the source 'οἰκείῳ τέλει' means a natural death, as opposed to martyrdom, and 'appointed' was ambiguous.
Changed 'Genesis 22:12' to 'Genesis 22:16': the quoted words 'οὐκ ἐφείσω... δι' ἐμέ' match Genesis 22:16 in the Septuagint.

problems.quote: For he ended his life by a natural end.
problems.source_quote: καὶ γὰρ οἰκείῳ τέλει τὴν ζωὴν κατέλυσε
problems.why: οἰκεῖος τέλος means 'his own end' (i.e., his proper destiny), not 'natural end' in sense of non-violent death.
problems.fix: For he ended his life by his own end.
problems.ruling: οἰκεῖος τέλος means 'his own end/destiny' (i.e., martyrdom as his proper calling), not 'natural end' (peaceful death); translator misread as 'natural' vs. 'his own', reversing the argument that he was a martyr by intention despite not dying violently.

problems.quote: living tombs, tombs that send forth a voice, tombs that are prepared for the same zeal
problems.source_quote: τάφους ἐμψύχους, τάφους φωνὴν ἀφιέντας, τάφους πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν ζῆλον παρασκευαζομένους
problems.why: 'prepared for the same zeal' misrepresents παρασκευαζομένους: the tombs prepare/inspire others to the same zeal, not are prepared for it.
problems.fix: tombs that rouse others to the same zeal
problems.ruling: παρασκευαζομένους is middle/passive; 'prepared for zeal' is defensible, not clearly wrong.

παρασκευαζομένους is middle/passive but here means the tombs prepare or rouse others to zeal, not that they are prepared for it; changed to 'that rouse others to the same zeal'.

refereed.why: Chrysostom means Eustathius died a natural death (his own end came), not that he chose his death.
refereed.fix: he ended his life by a death of his own
refereed.ruling: οἰκείῳ τέλει means 'natural death,' not 'his own end'; 'by his own end' wrongly implies self-chosen death.

refereed.quote: For he ended his life by his own end.
refereed.source_quote: καὶ γὰρ οἰκείῳ τέλει τὴν ζωὴν κατέλυσε
refereed.why: οἰκείῳ τέλει means 'by a natural death,' not 'by his own end'; hides that he died naturally, not violently.
refereed.fix: For he ended his life by a natural death.
refereed.ruling: οἰκεῖον τέλος = natural death; 'by his own end' loses the key contrast with violent martyrdom.
